before.title: What's Really Inside an Atom?
before.descriptionLine1: Look at a gold ring, or the spoon beside your mug, or your own hand. How many times could you cut a piece of gold in half before it stops being gold? Across two hundred years, four experiments with weights, a glowing tube, a sheet of gold leaf and an X-ray bench opened the atom and fixed the periodic table.
before.description:
Look at a gold ring, or the spoon beside your mug, or your own hand. How many times could you cut a piece of gold in half before it stops being gold? Across two hundred years, four experiments with weights, a glowing tube, a sheet of gold leaf and an X-ray bench opened the atom and fixed the periodic table.

If you enjoyed this, subscribe for a new story from the history of science every week — and tell us in the comments which experiment surprised you most.

Chapters
0:00 Twenty-Eight Cuts of Gold
1:10 John Dalton Weighs the Elements
3:10 J. J. Thomson's Glowing Tube
4:40 Ernest Rutherford's Gold Foil
6:50 Henry Moseley's X-Ray Staircase
7:55 Mostly Empty Space

Further reading
- John Dalton, A New System of Chemical Philosophy (1808)
- J. J. Thomson, "Cathode Rays", Philosophical Magazine 44 (1897)
- Ernest Rutherford, "The Scattering of Alpha and Beta Particles by Matter and the Structure of the Atom", Philosophical Magazine 21 (1911)
- H. G. J. Moseley, "The High-Frequency Spectra of the Elements", Philosophical Magazine 26 & 27 (1913-1914)

after.title: What's Inside an Atom? Mostly Empty Space
after.descriptionLine1: What's inside an atom? Mostly empty space. This is the history of the atom in four discoveries, from cutting a gold coin to find the true size of an atom, to Rutherford's tiny centre and the number that fixed the periodic table.
